prompt: Why did DeepSeek's R1 release (January 2025) shock the AI industry and briefly crater tech stocks?
options: It was the first model to generate video
A Chinese lab released an open-weights reasoning model rivaling top US models, reportedly trained at a fraction of the assumed cost — challenging beliefs about compute moats
It was the first model to pass the bar exam
It leaked another lab's training data
explanation: R1 matched OpenAI's o1-class reasoning performance, was released open-weights under MIT license, and DeepSeek claimed strikingly low training costs. Markets read it as a threat to the 'only massive US compute spend wins' thesis — Nvidia lost a record ~$600B in market cap in one day.
nuance: The lasting effects: reasoning techniques diffused rapidly into open models, and 'efficiency' joined 'scale' as a competitive axis.
source_title: DeepSeek-R1 paper (arXiv) / The AI Daily Brief coverage

prompt: What happened to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) in 2025 that made it strategically significant?
options: It was deprecated in favor of plugins
Competing labs — including OpenAI and Google — adopted it, making it a de facto industry standard for connecting AI to tools and data
It became a paid enterprise product
explanation: Rival labs adopting a competitor's protocol is rare; OpenAI and Google embracing MCP in 2025 signaled the industry converging on shared agent-tooling infrastructure. For builders it meant one integration surface instead of per-vendor plugin systems.
nuance: Standards adoption is a strategic tell: interoperability layers tend to win when the ecosystem grows faster than any single vendor can.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — MCP adoption coverage

prompt: What was arguably the dominant AI product theme of 2025?
options: Agents — especially agentic coding tools (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor agents) doing multi-step work autonomously
explanation: 2025 was widely dubbed 'the year of agents': coding agents went mainstream, labs shipped computer-use and browser agents, and enterprises piloted agentic workflows. Coding was the breakout domain because outcomes are verifiable — code either runs and passes tests or doesn't.
nuance: The verifiability point generalizes: agents succeed first in domains with cheap, objective feedback loops.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — year in review

prompt: As pre-training gains slowed, what became the industry's major new scaling axis in 2024–2025?
options: Inference-time compute — letting models 'think longer' via extended reasoning, which improves results without retraining
explanation: OpenAI's o1 (late 2024) demonstrated that spending more compute at answer time — generating long internal reasoning — yields large gains on hard problems. Every major lab followed with reasoning modes, reshaping both capability roadmaps and inference-cost economics.
nuance: It changed infrastructure math too: inference (not just training) became a massive compute consumer, driving the 2025 datacenter buildout.
source_title: DeepLearning.AI — The Batch on test-time compute

prompt: The 2024 Nobel Prizes made AI history. Which is accurate?
options: Sam Altman won the Peace Prize
Geoffrey Hinton shared the Physics prize for neural-network foundations, and Demis Hassabis & John Jumper shared Chemistry for AlphaFold's protein-structure prediction
An AI system was itself awarded a Nobel
No AI-related work has ever won a Nobel
explanation: Two Nobels in one year went to AI: Hinton (with Hopfield) for foundational neural-network work, and DeepMind's Hassabis and Jumper (with David Baker) for AlphaFold, which solved protein-structure prediction — a decades-old grand challenge in biology.
nuance: AlphaFold is the standard answer to 'has AI actually advanced science?' — its predicted structures are used by millions of researchers.

prompt: What is the EU AI Act's core regulatory approach?
options: A blanket ban on generative AI in Europe
Risk-based tiers: banning 'unacceptable risk' uses, imposing strict duties on high-risk systems, and lighter transparency rules elsewhere — phasing in through 2025–2027
explanation: The AI Act (in force August 2024, phasing in over years) classifies AI by risk: social scoring is banned; high-risk uses like hiring and credit face conformity requirements; general-purpose models get transparency and systemic-risk duties. It's the world's most comprehensive AI law and a template others watch.
nuance: The recurring debate: whether it protects Europeans or handicaps European AI companies — expect this tension in any EU AI news you read.

prompt: The "Stargate" project announced in January 2025 is…
options: A massive US AI-infrastructure venture (OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle) pledging hundreds of billions for AI datacenters
explanation: Stargate, announced at the White House, committed up to $500B for US AI datacenters. It exemplified 2025's defining industrial story: compute infrastructure as national strategy, with capital spending at a scale comparable to historic infrastructure programs.
nuance: The buildout raised the follow-on debates you'll keep seeing: energy demand, circular vendor financing, and whether capacity is running ahead of revenue.

prompt: In mid-2025, Meta made headlines in the AI talent market by…
options: Forming a 'Superintelligence' lab and recruiting top researchers with reported nine-figure compensation packages
explanation: After a lukewarm Llama 4 reception, Zuckerberg personally recruited elite researchers (including Scale AI's Alexandr Wang) into Meta Superintelligence Labs, with offers reported in the $100M+ range — escalating an industry-wide talent war and signaling that top AI researchers had become the scarcest resource.
nuance: Talent-war stories are a useful lens on lab strategy: where the researchers move often predicts where capability moves.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — talent war coverage

prompt: Anthropic's Claude 4 generation (May 2025) leaned hardest into which positioning?
options: Coding and long-running agentic work — sustained multi-step tasks with tool use
explanation: Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 launched with emphasis on software engineering benchmarks and the ability to work autonomously for extended periods — aligned with Anthropic's Claude Code push and its enterprise coding-market strength.
nuance: Reading launches for positioning (not just capability claims) tells you each lab's revenue strategy: Anthropic → developers/enterprise, OpenAI → consumer scale + ecosystem, Google → integration everywhere.

prompt: What's driving the push toward small on-device AI models (Apple Intelligence, Gemini Nano)?
options: Small models are more intelligent than large ones
Privacy (data stays on device), zero-latency offline use, and no per-query cloud costs — worth the capability tradeoff for many everyday tasks
explanation: On-device models handle summarization, dictation, and assistance without sending data to servers — a privacy story (Apple's angle), a latency story, and a cost story. Hybrid designs route hard queries to cloud models while easy ones stay local.
nuance: Watch this boundary move: each generation of phone chips + model distillation pulls more capability on-device, shifting what needs the cloud at all.

prompt: OpenAI's GPT-5 launch (August 2025) was notable partly for its architecture choice. What was it?
options: A unified system with a router deciding per-query whether to answer fast or engage deeper reasoning — replacing the confusing model-picker menu
explanation: GPT-5 bundled fast and reasoning models behind an automatic router, ending the era of users choosing between confusingly-named models. The rocky rollout (complaints about routing quality and the beloved GPT-4o's removal) became a case study in AI product transitions.
nuance: The router concept matters beyond OpenAI: automatic capability-vs-cost routing is becoming standard architecture for AI products generally.

prompt: Why is AlphaFold considered a landmark AI achievement beyond just winning a Nobel?
options: It solved a 50-year grand-challenge problem — predicting 3D protein structure from amino-acid sequence — and its open database now accelerates drug discovery and biology research worldwide
It generated the first AI film
explanation: Determining a protein's structure used to take years of lab work per protein; AlphaFold predicts structures computationally with experimental-grade accuracy and DeepMind released predictions for essentially every known protein, used by researchers globally.
nuance: It's the flagship example of 'AI for science' — a category (materials, weather, math) many researchers consider AI's highest-upside application.

prompt: "Computer use" capabilities, which Anthropic first shipped publicly in late 2024, let models…
options: Operate a computer like a person — viewing the screen, moving the cursor, clicking, and typing — to complete tasks in real software
explanation: Computer use lets a model drive actual GUIs — the long tail of software with no API. Anthropic shipped it first in public beta (October 2024); browser-driving agents from other labs followed. It's a key unlock for agents doing real-world office work.
nuance: It remains slower and less reliable than API-based tool use — production agent designs prefer APIs where they exist and reserve GUI control for what has no better interface.

prompt: True or false: By 2025, training-data copyright questions were largely settled law in the US.
explanation: False. Major suits (NYT v. OpenAI, authors and music labels vs. various labs) were still working through courts, with mixed early rulings — some favoring fair-use arguments for training, others finding liability around pirated source copies, plus large settlements. The legal foundation of the industry remained genuinely unsettled.
nuance: Watch two separate questions courts keep splitting: whether training on copyrighted work is fair use, and whether outputs that reproduce it infringe — they can get different answers.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — copyright litigation coverage
